title: IgG4-Related Ophthalmic Disease (IgG4-ROD)
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to IgG4-Related Ophthalmic Disease (IgG4-ROD), a fibroinflammatory systemic condition that commonly masquerades as idiopathic orbital inflammation, thyroid eye disease, or lymphoma. This poster outlines the pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, histopathological hallmarks, and evidence-based management protocols essential for ophthalmologists.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: IgG4-Related Ophthalmic Disease (IgG4-ROD) is a distinct, immune-mediated fibroinflammatory condition characterized by tumefactive lesions that can affect any or all structures within the orbit. Clinically mimicking other inflammatory conditions, it is histopathologically defined by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis. It may manifest as an isolated ocular condition or as part of a wider, multi-organ systemic syndrome.

branches: Antigen Presentation (Unknown autoantigen/allergen triggers CD4+ T-cells)
Th2 & Treg Polarization (Upregulation of IL-4, IL-10, IL-13, and TGF-beta)
B-Cell Class Switching (IL-4 and IL-10 drive heavy chain switching to IgG4)
Fibrogenesis (TGF-beta activates myofibroblasts, causing storiform fibrosis)
Tissue Infiltration (Clonal expansion of CD4+ cytotoxic T-cells and IgG4+ plasma cells)

sections.title: The Histopathological Triad
content: Dense Lymphoplasmacytic Infiltrate: Abundant lymphocytes and IgG4+ plasma cells clustered in nests.
Storiform Fibrosis: Collagen fibers arranged in a characteristic whorled, 'woven-mat' pattern.
Obliterative Phlebitis: Fibrous obliteration of small-to-medium veins, often adjacent to intact arteries.
IgG4+ Cutoffs: >10-50 IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field (HPF) depending on tissue type, and an IgG4+/IgG+ ratio > 40%.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Ocular Manifestations
content: Painless Dacryoadenitis: Chronic, painless, firm, bilateral upper eyelid swelling (most common presentation).
Orbital Myositis: Thickened extraocular muscles (typically sparing the tendon insertions, mimicking Thyroid Eye Disease).
Infraorbital Nerve Enlargement: Pathognomonic sensory paresthesias or incidental V2 canal widening on imaging.
Scleritis & Episcleritis: Chronic, nodular or diffuse scleral inflammation, occasionally resistant to standard NSAIDs.
Compressive Optic Neuropathy: Rare but sight-threatening complication due to apical orbital crowding.

rows: Definite IgG4-ROD
At least 2 of 3 Triad features (Infiltrate, Storiform Fibrosis, Obliterative Phlebitis)
IgG4+/IgG+ ratio >40% AND >50 IgG4+ cells/HPF (or >10 for lacrimal gland)
Enlargement of lacrimal gland, extraocular muscles, or orbital mass
Probable IgG4-ROD
Suggestive lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate without typical fibrosis/phlebitis
IgG4+/IgG+ ratio >40% AND >10 IgG4+ cells/HPF
Bilateral lacrimal/orbital disease OR elevated serum IgG4 (>135 mg/dL)
Possible IgG4-ROD
Non-specific inflammatory infiltrate
IgG4+/IgG+ ratio <40% but elevated absolute counts
Compatible clinical presentation; other diagnoses excluded

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Serum Serology: Order total IgG, IgG subclasses (specifically IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4), and IgE. Serum IgG4 > 135 mg/dL is suggestive but not diagnostic.
Step 2: Orbital Imaging (CT/MRI): Assess for bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement, extraocular muscle hypertrophy, and infraorbital nerve (V2) canal expansion.
Step 3: Incisional Biopsy: Gold standard. Biopsy of the lacrimal gland or orbital mass is critical to rule out malignancy/lymphoma.
Step 4: Histopathology & IHC: Quantify IgG4+ plasma cells per HPF and determine the IgG4+/IgG+ ratio.
Step 5: Systemic Screening: Whole-body CT, PET/CT, or serum assays to check for subclinical salivary gland, retroperitoneal, pulmonary, or renal involvement.

rows: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
Tendon-sparing myositis; positive TRAb/TSI; bilateral upper eyelid retraction; no V2 nerve enlargement.
Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (IOID)
Acute, painful presentation; unilateral; rapid response to steroids but high recurrence; lacks systemic fibrotic lesions.
Sjögren Syndrome
Severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca; positive anti-SSA/SSB antibodies; lacks storiform fibrosis on minor salivary gland biopsy.
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)
Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; vasculitis; positive c-ANCA (PR3); prominent bony destruction.
Orbital Lymphoma (MALT)
Monoclonal B-cell population; light chain restriction; lacks dense IgG4+ plasma cell infiltration.

sections.title: First-Line Medical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Induction Therapy: Initiate Oral Prednisone at 0.6–1.0 mg/kg/day (typically 30–40 mg/day) for 2 to 4 weeks.
Step 2: Clinical Assessment: Monitor for reduction in proptosis, improvement in motility, and reduction in lacrimal gland size.
Step 3: Steroid Taper: Slowly taper prednisone by 5 mg every 2 weeks down to 5 mg/day, then slowly taper to zero over 3 to 6 months.
Step 4: Maintenance Therapy: If relapses occur during taper, introduce low-dose maintenance prednisone (2.5–5.0 mg/day) or transition to steroid-sparing agents.

sections.title: Second-Line & Steroid-Sparing Agents
sections.content: For patients with steroid-intolerant, steroid-dependent, or relapsing IgG4-ROD, steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents are indicated. Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) is highly effective, administered as 1g IV twice (2 weeks apart) or 375 mg/m² weekly for 4 weeks. Mycophenolate Mofetil (1.0–1.5 g BID), Methotrexate (15–25 mg weekly), or Azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) can also be used to maintain remission and avoid long-term corticosteroid toxicity.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags & Mimickers
content: Bone Destruction on CT: Highly suggestive of malignancy (e.g., Lacrimal Gland Carcinoma) or GPA; IgG4-ROD typically respects bone boundaries.
Rapidly Progressive Vision Loss: Indicates compressive optic neuropathy or orbital apex syndrome; requires urgent IV Methylprednisolone pulse therapy.
Monoclonality on Flow Cytometry: IgG4-ROD is polyclonal. Monoclonal populations indicate co-existing or misdiagnosed B-cell lymphoma.
Unilateral Painful Proptosis: Less typical for IgG4-ROD; always rule out acute IOID, orbital cellulitis, or ruptured dermoid cyst.

content.explanation:
I - Infraorbital nerve enlargement (V2 canal expansion on imaging)
G - Glandular swelling (painless, bilateral lacrimal and salivary glands)
G - Glucocorticoid responsiveness (rapid initial response to systemic steroids)
F - Fibrosis (storiform pattern on biopsy)
O - Obliterative phlebitis (venous occlusion on histopathology)
U - Unusually high serum IgG4 (>135 mg/dL)
R - Rituximab efficacy (highly targeted B-cell depletion therapy)

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Clinical Evidence
content: The Boston Consensus Criteria (2012): Established the definitive histopathological diagnostic guidelines for IgG4-RD, emphasizing that histopathology remains the gold standard over serum IgG4 levels.
The ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria (2019): Developed a validated point-based classification system for systemic IgG4-RD, incorporating clinical, radiologic, serologic, and pathologic features.

Rituximab Prospective Trials (Carruthers et al., 2015): Demonstrated that targeted B-cell depletion with Rituximab is highly effective for induction and maintenance of remission in IgG4-RD, even without concomitant steroids.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Do not rely solely on serum IgG4: Up to 30% of biopsy-proven IgG4-ROD cases have normal serum IgG4 levels.
Look at the bones: IgG4-ROD may cause remodeling of the orbital bones due to chronic pressure, but it does not cause bone erosion.
Rule out lymphoma: MALT lymphoma can mimic IgG4-ROD and can even arise within a background of chronic IgG4-related inflammation.
Always perform a systemic review of systems: Ask about dry mouth (submandibular glands), abdominal pain (retroperitoneal fibrosis), and dyspnea (pulmonary involvement).

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-Up
sections.content: While IgG4-ROD is generally highly responsive to systemic corticosteroids, the relapse rate after steroid taper is high (up to 30-40%). Long-term monitoring with periodic clinical exams, serum IgG4 levels, and orbital imaging is required. Patients with systemic multi-organ involvement require a multidisciplinary approach involving rheumatologists, nephrologists, and pulmonologists to monitor for silent but progressive retroperitoneal fibrosis or tubulointerstitial nephritis.
